call_history.summary: Rayfield called in distraught after witnessing his nephew, Denny, steal a catalytic converter from a respected, elderly rancher named Aurelio Serna. Rayfield had initially made Denny return the converter and threatened to call the police if it happened again, but he later discovered this wasn't Denny's first theft, realizing his nephew had been repeatedly stealing from Serna, who was quietly paying for the repairs himself. Rayfield grappled with whether to pay Serna back anonymously or tell him about the "man-made problem," ultimately deciding to have an honest conversation with Serna about security and another, more meaningful talk with Denny about his life choices, especially since Denny's mother recently lost her husband.

transcript.content: Rayfield, Rayfield, welcome to the show. What would you like to talk about today? How can we help you?
I watched my nephew steal from a man who has spent his whole life being decent, and I let my nephew walk.
What did he steal?

Catalytic converter. Off an old Tejano rancher's truck. Man named Aurelio Serna, his family's been running cattle east of Marathon since before this county had a name. And Denny — that's my nephew — was under that truck at two in the morning with a reciprocating saw.

Well, at least it was an election.  Okay, so your nephew stole this man's catalytic converter and you watched him at 2 o'clock in the morning?  What were you doing out at 2 o'clock in the morning watching him under a neighbor's vehicle?

I wasn't watching him do it on purpose. I was on my porch. Can't sleep most nights, I just sit out there. And I saw headlights pull up slow on Serna's property, which is not far from mine, and I knew those headlights. I know that truck. That's Denny's truck.
It looks like Marathon, Texas has a really long history of cattle ranching, going back to the 1800s, so Aurelio Serna's family being there for generations totally tracks.
Okay, and Rayfield, have you said anything to your nephew about this, or did you just kind of let it slide?

No I did not let it slide. I walked over there in my boots and my undershirt and I made him put it back. Stood over him while he reattached it. And then I told him if he ever did anything like that again I would call Brewster County myself. But here's what I didn't know then. This wasn't the first time.

Of course it wasn't the first time. I don't think it's... I've never done it myself, but I can't imagine it's easy to steal a catalytic converter. You have to know what it looks like, at least, and what to cut and wear so you don't ruin it. How do you steal a catalytic converter? Do you know?

Reciprocating saw and about four minutes if you know what you're doing. And Denny knew what he was doing. That's what got me. He wasn't fumbling around under there. He was practiced. And that's when I started putting it together — Serna had been replacing converters he thought were just failing on their own. Paying out of pocket. This man is not wealthy, Luke. He's land rich and cash poor like every rancher out here. And he's been bleeding quiet for months because of my nephew.
It's wild that he was so practiced, because most catalytic converter thefts happen overnight, usually between 6 P M and 9 am.
Okay, and does your nephew have a lot of cash? I mean, what's a catalytic converter worth on the used market these days?

Depends on the vehicle but you're talking anywhere from a hundred to maybe three, four hundred dollars at a scrap yard. And yeah, Denny had new boots. New boots and he just bought a used side-by-side. I didn't think anything of it at the time because he'd just started the job at the Gage. But that money wasn't coming from groundskeeping wages, I can tell you that.

Okay, so obviously, you talk to him about it, and he knows that you know now, and how did he respond when you told him not to do it anymore?  You were going to call the cops.  You know what they say about snitches, right, Rayfield?

He was ashamed. I'll give him that. He didn't argue with me, didn't try to explain it away. Just got quiet and nodded. But here's the thing I haven't told anybody — I kept my mouth shut partly because Denny's mother, that's my sister Carol, she buried her husband eighteen months ago. And I cannot put her through losing her son to the county jail on top of that. I just cannot do it. So, maybe that's why I did what I did.

Well, it makes sense that you wouldn't narc out your own family for doing something like that, but maybe you could talk to the rancher and let him know what's going on.  So he's probably got suspicions if he's replaced a few of these, and your nephew there has been at this over and over again.  Maybe you could tell him to put up some cameras, give him a little hint that maybe he's got somebody on his property, taking his stuff.  and do you have a camera at your property, like a doorbell camera or something like that that can catch that area?

No cameras out here. This is Highway three hundred eighty five country, Luke, it ain't a subdivision. But what you're saying about talking to Serna — I've been turning that over. I got four hundred dollars in an envelope on my kitchen table. Been sitting there eight days. I was going to mail it to him anonymous. But I keep thinking — that man deserves to know it wasn't his truck failing him.

Well, I mean, I'm out here too. There are plenty of cameras. There's trail cameras. There's traffic cameras. There's cameras all over the place, even out here. So to think that there's not as naive. It wouldn't be expensive or difficult to throw up a trail camera to keep track of your ranch property. I think probably most ranches have at least some cameras somewhere for just this reason. But no, I don't think that you should pay  him. You didn't steal it. And it's protecting his property is his own responsibility. So you should keep your money, but it wouldn't be wrong of you to walk over there and sort of give him the hint. You don't have to knock out your nephew for doing it. Obviously, he knows that you know and he's not going to do it anymore. But let him know that he should have some lighting out there and some basic security.  cameras because they're they're not expensive. And in 2026, it makes a lot of sense to have that.

You know, what, that's — that lands different than I expected it to. Because I've been so fixed on the money, like money was the thing that would settle it in my chest. But you're right that it wasn't my debt to pay. The debt is Denny's. And maybe what I actually owe Serna is a conversation, not an envelope. The Rocking S brand has been on cattle in this county longer than most families have been here. That man deserves to hear a truth, even if it's a partial one.

Yeah, keep it a partial one. You don't have to say any names. You don't have to say even that you saw it, just to bring it up that, you know, you seem to be having problems with missing catalytic converters that looked like they were sought out by a reciprocating saw. And I think maybe that was a man-made problem.

That's a decent way to put it. Man-made problem. I could say that much without saying Denny's name. Just neighbor to neighbor. Let him know it wasn't his truck. Let him know to put a light out there, maybe a camera like you said. That's — I can do that. That's something I can actually do. And maybe that envelope stays on my table a little longer. Or maybe I hand it to Denny and tell him he's going to find a way to make this right himself, even if Serna never knows where it came from.

I just looked it up, and while the numbers are down from their peak in twenty twenty two, there were still over twenty six,000 catalytic converter thefts in the first half of twenty twenty three alone.
I think you meant to say 26,000 catalytic converter thefts, and that's quite a few.  What is it in the catalytic converter that's worth the money to the scrapyard?  What sort of metal?

Platinum. Palladium. Rhodium. Those are the metals in the catalyst itself. Rhodium especially got sky high a few years back. That's what drove the whole wave of it. Denny knew that. He's not stupid, that's the hell of it. He's just — he made a bad choice and then he kept making it because nobody caught him.

Well, I'm not stupid either, and I didn't know that a catalytic converter contained rhodium, and that rhodium was a, I don't even know what rhodium is. It sounds radioactive. What is rhodium and what else is it used in that it can command such a high price? Is it just other catalytic converters? Because then why take it to a scrapyard and not just resell the catalytic converter?

Rhodium's a platinum group metal. It's used in catalytic converters, some jewelry, certain industrial processes. It's rare. A few years back it was worth more per ounce than gold by a significant margin. And as for why scrap it instead of resell — a used converter off a specific truck is traceable if somebody's looking. Scrap yard melts it down, nobody's asking questions, cash in hand same day. That's the whole business model. Denny wasn't selling parts. He was selling metal he didn't own.

Yeah, I get that. But if it's so rare, how can it be in catalytic converters? I mean, trucks, cars are not rare. So there's obviously quite a few of them out there on the road. I don't know if you've looked around recently. So it can't be that rare.

It's rare in concentration. There's not much of it in any one converter — we're talking fractions of a gram. But you aggregate enough of them, it adds up. That's why these operations, the serious ones, they're not stealing one or two. They're running volume. Denny was running volume on one old man's truck and that's — that's what I keep coming back to. He picked Serna specifically.

Why do you think that is? Well, you're talking about Marathon, Texas. There's only like 300 people there, right? So there's not a whole lot of other people to pick besides Serna. But it sounds to me like you need to have a conversation with this man and let him know that it's time to get some lighting and some cameras out. And that's the best you can do. Keep your money. You didn't steal anything. You don't owe that money and you probably need it just as much as Serna does.

You're probably right about the money. And Marathon's small enough that Denny picking Serna wasn't random. Serna's property sits off a dark stretch with no traffic at two in the morning. Easy in, easy out. Denny did the math on that. And that bothers me more than the stealing itself, almost.

Well, then maybe it sounds like you need to have another conversation with Denny and talk to him about what he's doing and how that affects real people's lives because he's just a kid. He doesn't think like that. I didn't think like that when I was a kid. Stealing stuff wasn't an issue for me because I didn't have that part of my, I guess, brain developed yet to understand or to put myself in the shoes of the victim of the theft. Now I wouldn't imagine stealing from somebody, but when I was 16, it was,  wasn't a thing that made my conscience, it did not engage my conscience in any way.

He's twenty-two though. That's old enough to know. But I hear what you're saying — maybe he hasn't fully connected it to Serna the man, the family, the four generations. He just sees a truck on a dark road. Maybe that's the conversation I need to have with him. Not the one I already had, which was mostly me standing over him angry in my undershirt at two in the morning. A real one.

Yeah, 22 is a bit old to be doing that sort of stuff, but you should talk to him and see what he's doing with the money, if there's drugs involved or what the deal is, and do what you can to let him know that what he's doing is affecting real people's lives, honest, hardworking people that have, you know, they don't have much, so taking from them is extra bad.

I don't think it's drugs. Denny drinks some but I've never seen him strung out. I think it might be simpler and sadder than that — I think he wanted the side-by-side and the boots and to feel like he had something. His daddy's gone and he's twenty-two and he's raking leaves at a hotel. That don't excuse it. But I think that's what it is.
I just looked up rhodium again, and it's actually one of the rarest and most valuable precious metals, even more so than gold or platinum.
Wait a second. He's at the Gage Hotel in Marathon, Texas, rakingly. There's no trees in the desert, sir. Where are the leaves coming from that he's raking?

Ha. Fair point. Groundskeeping. Whatever they have him doing out there. Watering the succulents, I don't know. The Gage is nice enough that somebody's got to keep it looking that way. But yeah, leaves might have been a stretch.
Wait, I just looked up the Gage Hotel, and they actually have twenty seven acres of gardens with trees and plants, so there would definitely be leaves to rake.

be damned. I wouldn't have thought that at all. I've never been to the Gage Hotel, but I hear it's a wonderful place.  Okay, well, thank you for the call, Rayfield. I think you need to have a couple of conversations there.  Talk to Denny about his life choices and talk to your neighbor about security cameras  and identifying man-made problems with his truck.

I appreciate it, Luke. I came on here thinking I needed somebody to tell me I did right by keeping Denny out of jail. But I think what I actually needed was somebody to point me toward the next thing to do instead of just sitting with it. I'll talk to Serna. And I'll talk to Denny. A real talk this time. That envelope can wait.

call_history.situation_summary: Rayfield's dilemma is eight days old and he cannot stop thinking about it. He caught his nephew, Denny — twenty-two, just got hired on at the Gage Hotel as a groundskeeper — stealing a catalytic converter off the truck belonging to an elderly Tejano rancher named Aurelio Serna, whose family has run cattle east of Marathon for four generations. Rayfield saw it happen from his porch at 2 a.m. He didn't call the police. He confronted Denny himself, made him put the part back before Serna noticed it was gone, and kept it quiet. But then he found out that Denny has been doing this for months — this was not a first time — and that old Serna has been paying out of pocket to replace converters he thought were just failing on their own. Rayfield knows Serna. He knows the man cannot easily afford this. He kept his nephew out of jail and now he is not sure he had the right to do that with someone else's losses.
call_history.communication_style: Low, contained, ashamed — the voice of a man who has not slept clean in a week and is only calling because the envelope has been sitting there for six days
key_details: Aurelio Serna's family brand is the Rocking S and his great-grandfather trailed cattle through Marathon before the county was even organized
Rayfield kept the confrontation quiet partly because Denny's mother — Rayfield's sister — buried her husband eighteen months ago and Rayfield cannot stand the thought of breaking her again
He has $400 in an envelope on his kitchen table that he intends to mail anonymously to Serna but has not yet mailed

call_history.summary: The caller discussed seeing the Marfa Lights, specifically questioning their distance and movement. The host, who had previously mocked believers, was deeply unsettled by experiencing the lights for 11 minutes, describing them as holding a fixed position before moving laterally with "zero deceleration," and expressed frustration with inadequate scientific explanations like the plasma vortex theory, emphasizing the lights' ability to go behind mountains.

transcript.content: How far away was that light from the viewing area? So the viewing area is just like a building that you stand out on and look out over the desert, and there's lights out there that do unexplain things, and they've been there for a long time. A lot of people have seen them and talk about them, and nobody can come to a consensus on what they're about, right? So how far off into the distance did you see these lights?

I have lived here four years and made fun of the lights people and I owe every single one of them an apology. Okay, so — the viewing area faces south-southwest, and the lights were out over the Mitchell Flat area, which I think is roughly eight to ten miles out? But here's the thing, and this is what I keep getting stuck on when I try to explain it to people — the distance is actually part of what messed me up. Because at that distance, a light that holds a fixed position for eleven minutes and then moves laterally with zero deceleration, like, no ramping up, no curve, just — it's there and then it's somewhere else — that's not a car. That's not a ranch vehicle. I know what headlights do at eight miles in the dark. I grew up on the Gulf Coast, I know flat land, I know how light travels over flat land at night.
So, I just looked up Mitchell Flat, and it's actually described as where the Marfa Lights are most often seen, and it's known for being incredibly flat.

Okay, so if you don't think that these were headlights, what do you think they were? You're the one that saw them, so what is it that you, do you think it was aliens? Do you think it was government testing, like military stuff? What's your assessment?

Okay, so that's the question I've been sitting with for two days and here's my honest answer — I don't know, and I'm actually okay with that. What I'm not okay with is the explanations that are supposed to close the case. I read the University of Texas at Dallas study, the plasma vortex thing, and look, I'm not a scientist, I dye fabric for a living, but — a plasma vortex does not drop behind a mountain range and reappear on the other side. That's not what plasma does. That's not what any atmospheric phenomenon I've ever heard of does. So, do I think it was aliens? I mean.
Okay, I'm not a scientist either. What does plasma generally do? What would you expect a, I don't know what a fucking plasma vortex is. What would you expect a plasma vortex to do?

Right, okay, so from what I read — and again, I am a textile person, so take this with a grain of salt — a plasma vortex is basically ionized gas that gets trapped in like a rotating air mass, and it glows. And the argument is that the temperature differentials over Mitchell Flat create these conditions where you get these glowing gas pockets that drift and split and kind of do weird things. And I'll grant you, that actually does explain some of what I've seen the other three times I've stopped there. Like, drifting, merging, that stuff — fine, maybe. But one of these lights on Tuesday night held completely still. For eleven minutes. I timed it on my phone. And then it moved — not drifted, moved — laterally, fast, and was just gone.
Are you sure that it moved and it wasn't just a different light that popped up somewhere else that was the same size and shape?  What color were the lights that you saw?

That is — okay, that's a genuinely good question and it's the one that keeps me up at night a little. I can't be a hundred percent certain. I was watching it, I was focused on it, but it's dark and it's far away and I'm standing in a parking lot with wet indigo containers in the back of my Subaru. So, I can't swear to you in a court of law that it was the same light that moved versus a different light appearing. What I can tell you is that there was a continuity to it visually that felt like motion rather than replacement. But you're right to poke at that. The colors — they were mostly white-yellow.
White yellow? White or yellow? Were they white or were they yellow? Or were they just a warm white?

Warm white. Like, not the blue-white of an L E D, not orange like a sodium lamp. Warm white. But one of them, the one that went behind the Chinati Mountains and came back, that one had a moment where it went — I want to say amber. Like genuinely amber, not just warm white. And that was brief, maybe thirty seconds, and then it was back to the same warm white as the others. And I noticed it because I was already watching so hard by that point. I had been pulled over for maybe twenty minutes at that point and I was just — I was locked in.

Okay, well, I think I'm going to have to check out these Marfa lights for myself because I've read lots of different types of reports and explanations for what they are. But I haven't seen them myself. When you were there, when you were checking this out, were you alone or were there a bunch of other tourists there with you?

There were two other cars. One couple, they were there when I pulled in, and they left maybe fifteen minutes into it. Which, I still don't understand that. They just got back in their car and drove away. And then there was a guy, older, he had a camp chair, like he had planned this, he had brought a camp chair and a thermos. And he and I didn't really talk much, we were both just watching. But at the end, when it was winding down, I went over to him and I said, did you see that one go behind the mountains, and he just nodded. Like it wasn't even a question.
I'm seeing that the Wikipedia article mentions scientists concluded the lights were car headlights, but also that they're described as an "optical phenomenon.
The Wikipedia article also mentions that the Marfa lights are an optical phenomenon regularly observed near Marfa, Texas, and that the community has publicized a viewing area to encourage tourism.
Is it possible that the community of Marfa, they're clever people out there, Marfa's a clever little town, could they have staged these lights for the purpose of tourism?

Ha. Okay. I mean, I love Marfa, but we can barely get the coffee shop to stay open consistent hours. We are not coordinating an elaborate light show eight miles out over a private ranch in the dark on a Tuesday night when I happened to be driving back from Alpine. Like, the infrastructure for that conspiracy does not exist here. But also — the lights have been reported since the 1880s. Before cars.
That's wild that they've been reported since the 1880s, before cars were even around, which totally debunks that theory about headlights.

Yeah, it's hard to believe that there are headlights. I mean, what road is even back there? Is there a road back there, or are they just supposed to be headlights out in somebody's ranch, like off-road?

There's one highway, Highway sixty seven going toward Presidio, and yeah, people say it's those headlights refracting over the flat. But sixty seven runs in a pretty consistent line and what I saw was not consistent with anything running in a line. And here's the thing I haven't told you yet — at one point there were six distinct lights simultaneously. Not two, not three. Six. Separated, doing different things, different speeds.
I'm seeing that accounts of the Marfa Lights often describe them as floating orbs—white, yellow, or orange—drifting or flickering, and sometimes multiple lights are seen simultaneously.
All right, well, I'm going to have to see these lights for myself.  It does sound like the plasma vortex thing could be, they could be on to something with that.

I mean, maybe for some of it. I'm willing to give them some of it. But Luke, you should go. Genuinely. Go on a clear night, not too much moon, and just — give it an hour. The mistake I made the first three times was I gave it like ten minutes and left. Tuesday I stayed because I couldn't make myself get back in the car.

I just looked it up, and while the "plasma vortex" is a theory, other scientific explanations include atmospheric refraction, piezoelectric effects from tectonic stress, and even bioluminescent animals.

What bioluminescent animals are out here in the desert? Isn't that like a deep in the ocean kind of thing? I mean, we don't have fireflies or anything like that. There's no, like, bioluminescent mushrooms or fungi. Are there any bioluminescent animals in the desert out here?

I mean, I'm not a biologist either but no. No. I dye fabric with plants and I spend a lot of time thinking about what the land out here produces and I have never once seen anything glowing in the Chihuahuan Desert. And even if there were — six lights, eleven minutes stationary, behind a mountain range and back. No animal does that. That explanation is so much worse than just saying we don't know.
Well, I have seen some actually glowing bugs. They're bigger than fireflies. They're not flies. I don't know what they are, but they have like little lights on their backs around here.

Wait, really? I have not seen that. What do they look like? Because now I'm going to be second-guessing every small thing I see at night for the rest of my life, which is not helpful. But also — even if that's true, even if there are glowing beetles or whatever out here, that does not scale up to what I saw Tuesday. Like, a bioluminescent bug does not hold position for eleven minutes and then accelerate laterally.
Wait, I just looked this up, and apparently, the most common scorpion in Texas, the Striped Bark Scorpion, actually glows under U V light, but it's not bioluminescent in the way we're talking about.

Well, I thought that all scorpions glue if you hit them with a black light. I noticed that in Utah, too, we brought out a black light to check for scorpions when we went camping, and it totally works. They look super cool.  But what I'm talking about is more like a cricket kind of bug or some sort of a beetle that has a little glowy light on it, and they're pretty cool.

Okay, that's actually fascinating and I've been here four years and never encountered that, so now I have a whole separate thing to look into. But I want to make sure I'm not getting completely derailed by glowing beetles because — the point I keep coming back to is that I saw something I cannot explain, and I've been showing this terrible useless video to everyone in Marfa for two days and getting shrugged at, and I just needed to describe it out loud to someone who would actually sit with the forty minutes. And you have done that. So, thank you.

Can you send us that video? Can you email it to submissions at Luke at the Roost, please? I'd like to see it myself.  And I'm not surprised if you're showing that to people in Marfa. They've all seen the lights before, so it's not a new thing to them. They're pretty familiar with it.

Yeah, I will send it. Fair warning, I have already told you it's bad, but it's genuinely bad. Like, it looks like a black rectangle with some pixels. My phone just could not handle the low light at that distance. But I'll send it. And you're right about Marfa, that's exactly it — everyone here has either seen them and made peace with not knowing, or they've decided it's headlights and closed the door on it. Nobody wants to sit in the uncertainty with me. The guy with the camp chair came closest.

Well, I'm going to go check it out myself, and my camera is able to see pretty well in the dark, because I do the astro photography stuff.  So I'll see if I can catch that, and maybe we'll get to the bottom of this and figure out what the Marfa lights are once and for all here at Luke at the Roost.

Please do. And when you go, give it a full hour minimum. Don't leave after fifteen minutes like a tourist. And if you catch something on that camera that actually shows what they're doing — the splitting, the lateral movement, the way they just stop — I will buy you a coffee and also possibly cry a little. I'm genuinely invested in this now. Four years of skepticism and one Tuesday night completely undid me.

Okay, just one more thing before we move on. Just hypothetically, if this is extraterrestrial activity or supernatural activity, what do you think they could be doing? Why Marfa and what are some potential things that you could imagine these lights were actually doing?

Okay, hypothetically. If I let myself go there — Marfa is in one of the darkest, most remote stretches of land in the continental United States. If you wanted to observe without being observed, this is where you'd do it. And there's something about the Chinati Mountains specifically, there's a lot of mineral density in that range, copper, silver, there's mining history all through there. So, if I'm spinning a theory — maybe it's not about us at all. Maybe whatever it is isn't interested in the viewing area or the tourists or me standing there with my indigo. Maybe we're just incidental to something that was happening here long before the 1880s and will keep happening after we're gone. That actually makes me feel better somehow rather than worse.

is they could be mining or extracting minerals from the area. I mean, I do the astrophotography work, so I've been to a lot of places in the continental United States that are as dark as Marfa is. It's not the only place, and there's more people there than in a lot of stretches of remote Utah or Wyoming, or there's a lot of even less populated dark places. So it's probably,  Probably not because they don't want to be seen.  There's, I mean, there's a viewing area to see them, and it's been there for a long time, so that doesn't make sense.  But if there is some sort of mineral there that is not available in other places, like rhodium, perhaps, maybe that's what they're doing, and the lights are a mining operation from the aliens.

Alien rhodium mining. I'm going to be thinking about that every time I drive past the Chinatis now, thank you for that. But actually what you said about it not being about avoiding people — that's kind of the thing that unsettles me most when I sit with it. They're not hiding. Whatever those lights are, they have never hidden. They've been visible from the road for over a hundred years. That's either total indifference to us or something else entirely, and I don't know which one is more unsettling.
Maybe they're out there trying to steal catalytic converters.
That would actually explain the lateral acceleration. Get in, get out, no deceleration curve. Very efficient catalytic converter operation. I respect the hustle.

call_history.situation_summary: Suki is not calling about a crisis. She is calling because two nights ago she witnessed the Marfa Lights — actually witnessed them, a full display, not a smear of headlights — and what she saw does not match any of the standard explanations she has since read, and she is genuinely, delightedly unnerved. She pulled off at the official Marfa Lights Viewing Area on Highway 90 on her way back from a supply run to Alpine, and the lights performed for nearly forty minutes: splitting, rejoining, hovering, one of them dropping straight down behind the Chinati Mountains and then reappearing on the other side. She has seen the lights three times before and dismissed them. This time she took video on her phone. The video, she says, is terrible — it looks like nothing — but she knows what she saw. Saw an article about a Cleveland mayoral candidate who believes good leaders serve the mission and their team, and it's been on their mind.
call_history.communication_style: Bright, a little giddy, self-aware about the irony of her conversion, genuinely excited — this is the best thing that has happened to her in months
key_details: She was driving back from picking up an order of indigo and black walnut hull from a supplier in Alpine when she stopped — she still had wet dye containers in the back of her Subaru
One of the lights held a fixed position for what she timed at eleven minutes before accelerating laterally with no deceleration curve
She has since read the University of Texas at Dallas plasma vortex explanation and finds it insufficient for what she observed

call_history.summary: A sheriff's deputy called in, distressed about dashcam footage showing his partner making an unlogged stop at a known meth distributor's house. He was torn between loyalty to his partner of six years and his duty, fearing both accusing an innocent friend and covering for a potentially corrupt one, but ultimately decided to confront her directly.

transcript.content: Gus, welcome to the show.  What's going on out there in your life tonight?  How can we help?

There's a piece of dashcam footage I've watched eleven times that I'm probably going to watch eleven more times tonight instead of doing anything about it. I'm a sheriff's deputy. Fifteen years. And I found something on footage from my partner's patrol car three weeks ago that I don't know what to do with. And I haven't told anybody. Not my supervisor, not my wife, nobody. You're the first person I've said this out loud to.
Okay, what is it that you saw on the dash cam?

My partner made an unlogged stop. Thirty minutes. House on the north edge of town. And I know whose house it is. The man who lives there has ties to a meth distribution pipeline that runs up from the border through our county. Now — she's not under investigation. She has family on that street.
It's wild how common these meth pipelines are, I'm seeing headlines about busts from San Antonio to the Capital Region, and even Little Rock.

All right, so if you're familiar with the house and you know that there's a meth operation there, why are they not under investigation?  Yeah, I mean, taking your partner out of this completely just for a second, how can you, in good conscience, know that that's going on at that place without doing anything about it?

That's a fair shot. The honest answer is the guy — Cecil — he's known. The department knows about him. He's not a secret. He's just, he's slippery. The kind of person who's connected enough to the pipeline that you know he's there but building a case on him is a different unit's problem, a different jurisdiction's problem. He's not my case. So, I'm not sitting on some bombshell about Cecil specifically.
Okay, all right, so back to your partner. How long has this been your partner?

Six years. And she trained me before that, when I first came on. So, we're talking about somebody who — she drove two hours in the dark once to help me change a tire after a chase that went bad. That kind of partner. That kind of person. At least that's who I thought I knew.

Okay, so she's a friend of yours, you would say, right? You'd categorize her as a friend. It seems like you could have a conversation with her about this and say, look, I found this on the dash cam. I'm curious, like hear her side of the story. Maybe there's a good explanation for her being at this guy Cecil's house.

Yeah. Yeah, that's the obvious move and I know it. But here's where I get stuck — if she's clean, I've just told my partner of six years that I suspected her of running with a meth distributor. That doesn't go away. We still have to get in that car together every shift. And if she's not clean...

Well, no, it doesn't say you suspected her of anything. If you suspected her, then you probably would have anonymously sent that footage into your supervisors or something of that sort. If you instead go to her and say, hey, look, you know, I found this on the dash cam, and it seems odd to me, can you explain what you were doing here? You might get a positive answer or one you're not expecting. If she's not clean, then it's a completely different story, and it's a different decision for you.  and you have to decide if you want to keep that under wraps and protect your friend or if she's in trouble or possibly being blackmailed or something like that and needs your help or if she's a criminal and needs to be turned in.

The blackmail angle. I hadn't — I mean I thought about it for a second and then I moved past it but you're right, that's a real possibility out here. Cecil is exactly the kind of person who would have something on somebody and use it. And if that's what's happening to Terri, then me going to a supervisor without talking to her first, I've just blown up her life and she's the victim. Okay. You're making me think talking to her first is the right call.

Yeah, talking to her first is obviously the right call, because, I mean, think about it, she trained you, she's been doing this for a long time, she knows she's got a dash cam. She obviously left that on purpose, maybe trying to lead you a breadcrumb to crack the case.  But if she was doing some sort of off-color activity, if she's involved in some way, she wouldn't use her service vehicle and leave the dash cam on to go there, would she?

That's — okay that actually hit me. That's a good point. She's been on the job long enough to know exactly what that camera captures. She knows the logging system. She knows the purge schedule. If she wanted to hide something she would have taken her personal vehicle, she would have logged a break, she would have done a dozen things differently.

Yeah, it seems like she's either awful stupid or she wanted somebody to find this out and ask questions. So you should just talk to her next time you're on patrol or whatever and you know that you're in a safe space. Turn the body cameras off if you can or, you know, catch up with her for drinks after work and have this conversation somewhere private. Just talk to her about it. Ask her what's going on. Protect yourself and, you know, get to the  of it.

Yeah. Yeah, I think you're right. I've been sitting in my head with this for three weeks trying to find some perfect path that protects everybody and doesn't blow anything up and maybe the path is just — talk to her. She deserves that from me before anything else. After six years she deserves me looking her in the eye and asking the question instead of going around her. I've got twenty four days before that footage auto-purges. I don't have to decide tonight whether to preserve it formally.
Yeah, you got plenty of time. So do that. Is there anything else you'd like to talk about before we move on?

No, I think — I think that's it. You kind of cut through three weeks of me spinning my wheels in about five minutes. I'm going to call her tomorrow and ask if she wants to grab coffee before shift. That's where it starts. Thank you, Luke.

So, I just looked up police dash cam purge schedules, and it really varies a lot by department. some keep footage for months, others much less, but twenty four days is definitely within the normal range for non-evidentiary footage.

call_history.situation_summary: Gus's dilemma is about his partner on patrol, Deputy Terri Lujan, whom he has worked alongside for six years and considers a close friend. Three weeks ago Gus discovered, while reviewing dashcam footage for an unrelated incident report, that Terri had a thirty-minute personal stop — unlogged — at a house on the north edge of Fort Stockton that Gus recognizes. The house belongs to a man named Cecil Pryor, who Gus knows informally as someone connected to a methamphetamine distribution pipeline that runs up through Pecos County from the border. Terri is not under investigation. The stop may have been entirely innocent — she has family on that street, she could have had any reason. But Gus has watched that footage eleven times and the thirty minutes bothers him. He has not reported it. He has not asked her about it. He is sitting on it.
call_history.communication_style: Measured and careful — a man trained to describe facts without editorializing, but the control is costing him something
key_details: Terri Lujan trained him when he was a new deputy and once drove two hours in the dark to help him change a blown tire after a chase that ended badly — he owes her
The dashcam footage auto-purges after 45 days and he has 24 days left to decide whether to preserve it formally, which starts a process he cannot stop
He has a wife and two daughters and he keeps thinking about what it would do to his family if he reports a colleague and is wrong

call_history.summary: The caller, Concho, reports seeing mysterious vehicles mapping water sources on private ranches for nearly a year. He fears a large entity is compiling a secret inventory of water rights before making claims, and is frustrated that landowners dismiss his concerns. By the end of the call, Concho seems defeated, accepting that he's done all he can.

transcript.content: got Concho. Concho, welcome to the show. Thanks for calling Luke at the Roost. What's going on in your life tonight?
I have been building fence in this country for forty years and I know every road and every tank and something is mapping the water and nobody believes me.
What do you mean mapping the water? Like a submarine drone?

No no, on the ground. Vehicles. Trucks, SUVs, one time a sedan that had absolutely no business on a caliche road — I mean that car was scraping bottom. They carry cameras and what looks like survey equipment and they show up at stock tanks, at springs, at seeps. Places that are not on any public map. Places I only know because I have been stringing wire on these ranches for decades.

What do you mean they're not on a public map? We have GPS, right? So, I mean, the map of everything out there outside of military bases is going to be mapped. So maybe it's just like Google Maps going out there, sending their cameras.

Google Maps is not driving a gray S U V down a two-track caliche road to stand at the edge of a stock tank with a laser rangefinder. That is not how Google Maps works. And I know what government survey crews look like — I have worked alongside usgs crews, I know their trucks, I know their equipment, I know how they operate. They stop and talk to you. They have paperwork. These people do not stop. Every single time I have come up on one of these vehicles, they are gone before I can get to the gate. And I am not talking about G P S coordinates on a satellite image.
Well, if you can't get up to them, how do you know that they have laser range finders?

Fair point. I saw it once. Got close enough once — fella was standing at the edge of a tank outside of Marathon, had what I recognized as a rangefinder, the kind you use for surveying distance and elevation. That was the one time I got within maybe two hundred yards before he got back in his truck. The other times I am going off cameras on tripods, which I can identify from a distance, and the fact that these are not people who are lost. Lost people stop and ask directions. These people know exactly where they are going.

Okay, so that could be lots of things. It's not unheard of for people to survey water sources. I mean, that could be the town or the county. That could be the state or federal government. There are water issues out here all the time. They're fixing broken wells, and somebody might just need an accurate accounting of all of the water wells and the plumbing in the county.  on to me.

Here is what does not fit that explanation. Three separate times, six weeks apart each time, I found somebody at the same spring outside of Sanderson. Same spring. That is not a broken well survey. That is not a county water inventory. That ranch has a year-round spring that the owner does not advertise — I mean he does not tell people about it, it is not on any document I have ever seen associated with that property. And somebody visited it three times in eighteen weeks with a six-week interval between each visit. That is monitoring. That is somebody tracking whether that spring is holding through the dry season.

Well, with all due respect, you install fencing, right?  So why would you be looking at the documentation of the property of somebody else's ranch?  This doesn't add up.  And I think have you talked to the landowner about the people that you've seen out on his land?  First of all, this is not your business.  Whatever it is, it's not your business.  You're there to install a fence.  And second of all, there could be a lot of very good reasons for somebody to be out there at that spring,  doing exactly what they're doing.

You are right that it is not my land. But when I am building fence on a man's property and I see strangers on that property, I think he deserves to know. And yes, I have talked to the landowners. That is exactly the problem. I have talked to ranchers directly, eleven months worth of talking, and I get smiled at and thanked and nothing happens. That is why I am calling you. Not because I want to be right about who is doing it.

Well, I'm still unclear as to why you're calling me, because it sounds like not a problem.  If the landowners and ranchers are okay with the people on their land, then they're okay with it.  It's their land, and then there's nothing to be concerned about.

They are not okay with it. They do not know it is happening. That is the difference. The rancher outside Sanderson does not know somebody has been to his spring three times. I have not been able to reach him directly — I was working a different section of that ranch for a neighbor, not for him. I am not his contractor. So, I cannot just walk up and knock on his door without it looking strange. And the ranchers I have told, they hear me out and they think I am seeing normal traffic. They are not taking it seriously because each individual sighting sounds like nothing. But I have twenty-two of them written down.

Okay, well, that's not what you said. You said you directly talk to him and you get smiled and thanked and nothing happens. I don't know what it is that you're expecting to happen, but let's just say that there is some nefarious activity going down around the water sources in Brewster County. What is it that you think could potentially be happening?

Water rights. That is what I think is happening. Somebody is building a private inventory of every viable water source in this part of Texas before they start making offers or filing claims. Because here is how it works — groundwater in Texas runs under rule of capture, meaning if you can pump it you can own it, and surface water runs under prior appropriation. If you are a large enough entity and you want to acquire water rights across a region, the first thing you need is a comprehensive map of where the water actually is. Not where it shows on paper. Where it actually is, whether it is holding, how much, what time of year. That is what this looks like to me. And once the acquisition starts it will move fast and the ranchers will be behind it before they know what hit them. I watched something similar kill a contract I had in two thousand nine and I have never forgotten it.
I don't understand how that's a problem.

Because these ranchers do not know they are being evaluated. If somebody is building a case for a water rights claim or a purchase offer, they are doing it with information the landowner does not have. That is not a fair negotiation. A man cannot protect what he does not know is being looked at. And some of these sources, like that spring outside Sanderson, may have legal questions attached to them that the owner has never had to think about because nobody has ever come after the water before. The day somebody shows up with a lawyer and a filing, that rancher is starting from zero and the other side has eleven months of data on him.

Why wouldn't the rancher know about the water on his property?  That seems like something the rancher would absolutely have the same information on.  He doesn't need to send a surveyor every six months.  And if there's going to be a purchase offer, that doesn't sound like a bad thing for the rancher, does it?

It might be a fine thing for one rancher who wants to sell. But water rights in this country are not just about the man who owns the land above the source. Once those rights get consolidated into a large private holding, every downstream user, every neighboring ranch that has been drawing from the same aquifer for three generations, they are all affected. And no, a rancher does not always know the full legal status of the water on his property. I know this because a water dispute in two thousand nine taught me more water law than I ever wanted to know. Most of these men know where their water is. They do not know what it is worth on paper, they do not know what claims could be filed against it, and they have never had to know because nobody came after it before. Now, somebody might be coming after it and the ranchers are not lawyered up and they are not ready.
Okay, and how is this your problem?

It probably is not my problem legally. But I have been on these ranches for forty years. I know these people. I have stretched wire with their fathers. That counts for something to me. And I will tell you honestly, I did not call tonight because I have all the answers. I called because I have a notebook in my glovebox with twenty-two dates and locations and vehicle descriptions and hand-drawn maps, and I have photocopied it twice because I do not want it to disappear, and I do not know what to do with it.

Show it to your friend's landowners. You said you've brought this to the ranchers and they just smiled and nodded. So obviously they don't have the same respect for you that you have for them. If you're trying to help them out and they don't want to listen, there's nothing more you can do for them, right? They don't want your help. They own their land and they think they're managing it well. And if they're not, then that's on them.

That lands harder than I want it to. You might be right. I have been chewing on this for eleven months and maybe I have made it my burden when it was never mine to carry. But here is the thing — I did not call tonight hoping you would solve it. I called hoping somebody with standing would hear it. A water rights attorney.

You can't hire a water rights attorney for a ranch you don't own on somebody else's behalf.  That's not your place to do. You're there to install a fence.  Now, if these are friends of yours and you want to give them the heads up that you've seen some strange activity going on in their property, that's one thing.  But if they choose not to listen to you or to brush it off, maybe they know about it or maybe they don't care.  Either way, you've done your part.
Yeah. Yeah, I hear you. I have done my part. I told them. They heard me. That is where my job ends. I think I knew that and just did not want to sit with it.

call_history.situation_summary: Concho is a true believer and he is calling dead serious. For the past eleven months he has been documenting what he believes is a coordinated, systematic effort to map and photograph every water source in the Trans-Pecos — stock tanks, springs, seeps, and seasonal plinths — by unmarked vehicles he has encountered on ranch roads where he works. He has logged twenty-two separate encounters. The vehicles are different each time: white pickup, gray SUV, a rented-looking sedan that had no business on a caliche road. They are always carrying survey equipment or cameras. They do not stop to talk. They are always gone before he can get to the nearest ranch gate. He does not believe this is government water surveying — he knows what that looks like, he has worked alongside USGS crews. He believes someone is building a comprehensive private inventory of every viable water source in this part of Texas ahead of a major acquisition or diversion action, and that the ranchers whose land these sources sit on do not know it is happening. Recently read about Trump getting indicted in Georgia for trying to mess with the 2020 election, and it's been on their mind.
call_history.communication_style: Deliberate, patient, the cadence of a man who has rehearsed this many times and knows he sounds like a crank and is going to make his case anyway
key_details: Three of his encounters were at the same spring — a reliable year-round source on a ranch outside Sanderson that the landowner considers private and does not publicize — on three different occasions six weeks apart
He has a notebook with dates, times, vehicle descriptions, and hand-drawn maps of the locations, which he keeps in the glovebox of his truck and has photocopied twice

Water rights in Texas are governed by the rule of capture for groundwater and prior appropriation for surface water — Concho knows this law better than most lawyers because a water dispute killed a contract he had in 2009

call_history.summary: A caller admits he hired a brilliant teacher who committed research misconduct by using data from his old study without citation. He struggles with the ethical dilemma, compounded by the fact she's about to present the same uncredited data at a conference, and ultimately decides to confront her privately before the conference, driven by respect for his former supervisor whose work she's using.

transcript.content: Desmond, what's going on, brother?
I helped hire someone I now think committed research misconduct, and she's the best teacher in our department, and I've been pretending I don't know for three months.
What is research misconduct?

She used data that wasn't hers without citing the source. Specific population estimates — mule deer, Trans-Pecos region — that appeared in her job application research summary. I recognized them because I worked on the original study as a postdoc. Those numbers don't just coincidentally match. That's not how wildlife population data works.
So is that basically a form of plagiarism? She used somebody else's study. It must have been published somewhere for her to get access to it, right?

Yeah, it's published. twenty nineteen, peer-reviewed journal. So, it's not like she had secret access to it — anyone could find it. Which almost makes it worse, because there's no excuse for not citing it. You don't just lift population estimates and present them in a job application like you generated that data yourself. That's — yeah, that's plagiarism.
Okay, so you've got an ethical issue there, and you hired this person, and you said that she's become your best teacher?

That's what makes this so hard to sit with. She's genuinely good. Like, I've heard students talk about her, I've seen how she runs her course — she's engaged, she's clear, she cares. And every time I see that, it just adds another layer of — I don't know what to call it. Guilt, maybe. Because I'm watching her build something here and I'm the only person who knows there's a problem underneath it.

Well, maybe you should reframe that problem.  How big of a problem is it, really?  She didn't steal the data.  I mean, it was publicly accessible published in a journal.  So she didn't cite the source.  That's wrong.  You could just talk to her about that and say, hey, you didn't cite the source.  But what are you really going to do about it?  Are you going to fire her because of it?  It seems a bit excessive.

That's — okay, that's actually the argument I've been making to myself for three months. And part of me wants to just accept it and move on. But here's where it gets complicated. She submitted an abstract for a regional conference in November using the same research. So, this isn't just something that happened once in a job application that's now in a drawer somewhere. It's ongoing. She's about to stand up in front of her professional peers and present work that includes data she didn't generate and isn't crediting.

Okay, well, here's where I'm getting stuck, because you said you worked on this data in some capacity, and you were familiar with it, and you reviewed her application, and you hired her.  So when you saw her application and you saw those numbers, you must have recognized them then, yet you hired her anyway.  So why did you do that?

I didn't recognize them then. I found them three months ago going through old conference proceedings for a completely unrelated paper I was writing. The application review was — there's a lot of material in those packets, and I wasn't cross-referencing against a twenty nineteen study I worked on years ago. When I saw those numbers in context, in the proceedings, sitting next to the original study — that's when it clicked. So, no, I didn't hire her knowing this.

No, I'm not really buying it. Something doesn't sound right about what you're saying. So you see these numbers on an application. You're like, wow, those are good numbers. It looks like you know what you're doing. And you hire the lady. Then some months later, you're working on another paper and you see the same numbers. And you're like, you know what? I recognize those numbers, not from when I worked on this study in 2019, but from this woman's application from three months ago. This sounds very strange and like maybe punitive on your behalf.  What is your relationship with this woman?

My relationship with her is nothing. She's a colleague I've known for four months. But I hear what you're saying, and I want to push back on the punitive part because that actually stings a little. The reason I recognized the numbers in the proceedings and not the application is that mule deer population estimates for the Trans-Pecos aren't something you just memorize. They're meaningful in context. When I was reading the proceedings, I was deep in that specific literature, and I saw the figures next to methodology I knew, framing I knew — and it clicked. In her application they were buried in a research summary paragraph without that context. But look — I'll grant you it sounds strange. I can't make it sound less strange. All I can tell you is that's what happened.

Well, it does sound strange because, I mean, it was buried in her application, yet you went back to her application to verify that these numbers were actually in her application, which would indicate to me that you've got something against this woman or you're looking into her to even find that.  So whether or not she's done anything wrong, it sounds like maybe she did. I don't, I'm not an academic. I don't understand the ramifications of not citing your research when that research is publicly available.  but it sounds like you've singled her out in some way for some reason, and I'd like to know what that reason is.

I went back to her application because I wanted to make sure I wasn't crazy. That's not singling someone out — that's due diligence before you blow up a colleague's career. And I don't have anything against her. I just told you she's the best teacher in the department. Why would I be sitting on this for three months, losing sleep over it, if I wanted to hurt her? But I want to address the other thing you said — about not understanding the ramifications in academia. It matters enormously. Your publications, your data, your research record — that's your entire professional identity in this field.

Okay, so what are you going to do with this information that you have?  You've seen her swiping other people's research and using it to advance her own career, and it sounds like you're going to do something, right?  You're either going to blow up her career or you're going to talk to her about it and see what's going on.  What is your plan?

I think I need to talk to her first. That's — I've been afraid to admit that's the right move because I kept telling myself it was just cowardice. Like I was looking for a way to avoid the formal process. But hearing it out loud, I think there's a real difference between giving someone a chance to explain and protecting yourself from a hard conversation. And there's a conference in November. That's a hard deadline. I can't let her walk into that room without saying something.
Why can't you?

Because the original study was led by my postdoc supervisor. He's at Texas A and M now. That's his work she's presenting without credit. And I respect that man enormously. I haven't talked to him in two years and I don't want the first conversation to be me calling him to say someone is using your data and I knew about it and said nothing.

Okay, well, talk to her. I mean, this sounds to me like something I wouldn't say anything to anybody about. I mean, it's not really your business at this point. If she's going to get called out for stealing people's research, then eventually she'll get hers. But you don't have to be the one that is the executioner here.

That's a tempting way to think about it. It really is. But I don't think I can unknow what I know. And the "eventually she'll get hers" path — that might mean she gets called out at the conference, in public, in front of her peers, by someone who isn't going to be as careful about how it lands. That's a worse outcome for her than me having a quiet conversation now. So, I think I'm going to talk to her. Just her.
All right, well, you do that, and I hope it goes well for you.
Yeah. Thank you. Honestly, just saying it out loud tonight helped me stop calling it mercy and start calling it the right thing. I'll set up a meeting Monday.

call_history.situation_summary: Desmond's dilemma happened three months ago and he has been carrying it under a professional smile since. He was on a search committee that hired a new colleague — Dr. Renata Voss, a wildlife ecologist who joined the department in May. Desmond was enthusiastic about her hire. Two weeks after she arrived, he realized, going through old conference proceedings for an unrelated paper, that a dataset in her job application research summary contained figures he recognized from a 2019 study by a team he worked with as a postdoc — figures that were not cited. The overlap is specific enough that it cannot be coincidence. He has not told the department chair. He has not told Voss. He has been watching her teach her first summer course and finding her genuinely excellent in the classroom, which is making it worse.
call_history.communication_style: Precise, intellectually organized, but increasingly unable to contain the ethical weight — a person whose professional identity is built on rigor and who is violating it by staying silent
key_details: The dataset in question involves mule deer population estimates in the Trans-Pecos region — Desmond's own specialty — which is why he recognized it immediately and why he cannot plausibly pretend he never saw it
Voss has already been invited to present at a regional conference in November and the abstract she submitted uses the same research
The original 2019 study was led by his postdoc supervisor, a man who is now at Texas A&M and who Desmond respects enormously and has not spoken to in two years

call_history.summary: Fern called in to express her surprise and emotional upheaval after visiting Donald Judd's aluminum boxes at Chinati, an experience that challenged her long-held dismissive views of the art. She was deeply moved by the changing light on the boxes, realizing the artist intentionally created a space for quiet contemplation, similar to how the desert naturally impacts her, leading her to appreciate the art and possibly apologize to her granddaughter and Judd.

transcript.content: Fern. Fern, welcome to the show. What's going on in your life tonight?
I went to look at some aluminum boxes this afternoon to humor my granddaughter and I came out a different person and I am not happy about it.
Aluminum boxes. What changed your life after seeing these aluminum boxes?

That is what I am trying to figure out. They're Donald Judd's — out at Chinati, in Marfa. I have driven past that place for thirty years calling it nonsense. I have said that out loud, to people's faces. And my granddaughter Lily dragged me in there today and I stood in one of those artillery sheds and something happened to me that I cannot account for.
All right, what is it that you saw and what happened to you?

It was the light. That's the part I can't get past. The sheds have these north-facing windows and the afternoon light was coming through and hitting the same box every few minutes in a completely different way. The box didn't move. Nothing moved. But it kept changing. And I stood there watching it happen and I did not notice forty-five minutes had gone by until Lily touched my arm. I have looked at this country my whole life.

Wait, so Donald Judd is considered the leading international exponent of "minimalism" and he wrote this essay called "Specific Objects" where he argued for a "rigorously democratic presentation without compositional hierarchy.
It's wild how much Donald Judd's work is tied to Marfa. he actually moved there permanently in the early 1970s and bought up a bunch of land and buildings to install his art.
Okay, so you saw the light dance off these aluminum boxes. Do you think that was an intentional design decision by the artist, or was it just a happenstance?

Oh it was intentional. That's part of what's making me so irritable about the whole thing. He put those windows exactly where he put them on purpose. He knew what that light was going to do. Which means he was doing what I thought only the land did — you know, the way the desert just works on you whether you invited it to or not. I spent fifty years thinking that was something you couldn't manufacture. And here is this man from New York who moved to my part of the world and put it inside a building and it still worked. Maybe worked harder.

Well, that's what artists do, right? They take the natural world and funnel it into a vision. They distill it into something that can be consumed by the masses. So it sounds like he was very successful.

Consumed by the masses" is where you're losing me a little. There was nobody in that shed but me and Lily for most of those forty-five minutes. It didn't feel like consumption. It felt more like — being caught. Like the thing had patience and it was just waiting for whoever walked in to finally hold still long enough. And I hold still plenty.

Well, he was an artist, and he bought all that land in Marfa and installed his art there for it to be seen by other people.  So whether or not there were other people there when you were there is pretty irrelevant, but his intention was for you to find that and for you to have that experience.

You're right. You're right, I'll give you that. He wanted exactly what happened to happen. That's not a trick then, is it. That's just — he made a thing that worked. Same as a good fence works. Same as a well-placed water tank works. You build it right and it does what it's supposed to do for whoever needs it, whether you're standing there watching or not. I never thought I'd be comparing Donald Judd to a water tank but here we are at eleven o'clock at night.
Actually, we're at 3.37 a.m. at night, but who's counting?

Well, that tells you something about where my head is. Lily is asleep and I've got cattle to move at six and I'm on the radio talking about aluminum boxes. Chalk is looking at me like I've lost my mind.
You know, it's actually 3 37 am right now, so Luke's even more off than he thought!
All right, well, thank you for the call. Is there anything else you'd like to talk about before we move on?

Just the one thing I came here to figure out. Why a person who has spent fifty years looking at the high desert — which is also mostly geometry and light — could walk into a building and be surprised by the same thing. And I think I just answered it myself. I had to hold still. Outside I'm always working. In that shed there was nothing to do but look. Maybe that's what the building was for. Maybe that's what Judd built. A place where you have no excuse not to hold still. I owe my granddaughter an apology and possibly I owe that man one too.

Well, I suppose that's what minimalism is all about, right? But I don't find it odd that you can suddenly see something special, magical, when you're in the right place, the right mindset. I mean, how many sunsets have you seen, but still you can be taken in awe by the right one at the right time?

That's a fair point. That's a genuinely fair point. I've seen sixty years of sunsets out here and last Tuesday one of them stopped me cold in the middle of feeding. Same sun. Same west. I didn't ask why that one hit different. I just let it.

I was just reading about Judd, and he actually said that the "new three-dimensional work doesn't constitute a movement, school, or style," even though he's considered the leading exponent of minimalism.

call_history.situation_summary: Fern is not calling about a crisis.
